Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Cold Temperature: Cold, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Rosa sat in the intake chair with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her posture rigid, as if she were bracing herself for something. She was a 42-year-old project manager, married for fifteen years, with two children in middle school. She had come to therapy not because she wanted to, but because her husband had told her, gently but firmly, that he could no longer watch her disappear piece by piece. Rosa herself was not sure what she wanted. What she knew, with a certainty that lived in her chest like a second heartbeat, was that her life had been destroyed and she would never get it back.

The event that had done it had happened eighteen months ago. Rosa had been diagnosed with a rare, aggressive form of bacterial pneumonia that had sent her into septic shock. She had spent twelve days in the intensive care unit, four of them on a ventilator. What she remembered of that time was not a smooth narrative but a series of fragments, each one cut off from the next. She remembered the cold of the emergency room—the way the gel on the ultrasound had felt like ice against her chest. She remembered the bright white of a needle going into her arm, and the sound of a monitor beeping too fast. She remembered a doctor’s face, calm and distant, saying words she could not understand. And then she remembered nothing. Hours, sometimes days, were simply gone. But the feelings—those had never left. Sometimes, without warning, she would be flooded with the full, suffocating terror of that first night in the ICU, the certainty that she was dying, the pressure in her lungs, the cold—always the cold—and she would be gasping on her living room floor with no image in her mind at all, just the raw, unbearable emotion. It was so extreme, she sometimes thought, that it could not have actually happened to her. It felt like a story about someone else, a movie she had watched, except that her body kept insisting otherwise.

In the months after her discharge, Rosa had tried very hard to put it behind her. She had told herself that she was lucky, that she had survived, that she should move on. But moving on, she discovered, meant policing her own mind. She had become vigilant, constantly watching her thoughts for any sign that she was losing control, that she was going crazy. If she caught herself remembering the hospital, she would force the memory away, trying to erase it entirely, as if she could scrub it from her brain. But the harder she tried not to think about it, the more the world seemed to remind her. The smell of antiseptic in a public restroom would stop her cold. A cold breeze from an air conditioning vent would make her heart race. And medical equipment—needles, IV lines, the white of a bandage—would send her into a silent panic that she had learned to hide behind a mask of composure.

Her job as a project manager had become a minefield. The office building had a floor of medical suites on the ground level, and she had started taking the stairs three flights up to avoid walking past the glass doors of the clinic. She had stopped going to the annual health fair. She had cancelled her own physical examination twice. When a colleague mentioned a routine blood test in a meeting, Rosa had felt the room tilt and had excused herself to the bathroom, where she had stood gripping the sink, telling herself she was not dying, she was not in the hospital, she was fine. But she did not feel fine. She felt, in her bones, that her body had been permanently damaged by what had happened. She was certain that she was more fragile now, that the next illness would finish her.

The most painful part, though, was what had happened to her role in the family. Before the illness, Rosa had been the one who held everything together—the schedules, the meals, the emotional temperature of the house. Afterward, she found herself unable to do any of it. She could not drive her children to the doctor for a simple check-up; she would pull over and ask her husband to take them instead. She could not sit through a parent-teacher conference if it was held in the school nurse’s office. She had become, in her own eyes, a failure in the most important role of her life. Her children had stopped asking her for help with their scraped knees. Her husband had started handling everything medical, from the dentist to the flu shot. Rosa watched them adapt to her absence, and she told herself that this was what she deserved.

She had come to therapy now because her husband had said, with tears in his eyes, that he missed her. Rosa did not know if she could be the person she used to be. She was afraid that the therapy itself would ask her to talk about the hospital, to remember the details she had spent so long trying to erase. But she was also afraid of staying like this—of living the rest of her life as a ghost in her own home, watching her family move on without her. She sat in the chair, hands still folded, and waited to see if anyone could help her find a way back.
